title: The Sun Says No to the Higgsino Explanation
hook: If a Higgsino caused LZ's odd recoil, the Sun would have been quietly hoovering up dark matter for billions of years — and IceCube would see the neutrinos. It doesn't.
key_points: A Higgsino is 'quasi-Dirac' when its two Majorana components are split by only a few MeV or less.
The Sun's gravity accelerates dark matter to about 1400 km/s in its core — fast enough to scatter inelastically off heavy nuclei.
Inelastic scattering makes the Sun an efficient trap: particles lose energy and fall onto solar-bound orbits.
Trapped Higgsinos annihilate to W and Z boson pairs, producing high-energy neutrinos that escape the Sun.
IceCube sees no such neutrino excess, which for the cosmologically preferred 1.08 TeV mass forces the splitting above 566 keV.
That excludes reading LZ's 248 keV event as endothermic inelastic Higgsino scattering on xenon.
content_html: A neat feature of dark matter models is that they usually predict more than one thing. The proposal that LZ's unexplained 248 keV recoil came from an inelastic Higgsino has a second, unavoidable consequence: the same interaction would let the Sun capture dark matter very efficiently. A new analysis follows that thread and finds it does not survive.
extra_html: Inelastic scattering costs energy — the incoming particle has to convert into a slightly heavier partner state — so it only happens above a speed threshold set by the mass splitting. Dark matter falling into the Sun is accelerated to roughly 1400 km/s in the core, far faster than typical galactic speeds, which switches the reaction on and lets the Sun trap particles onto bound orbits. Those trapped Higgsinos then annihilate into W and Z boson pairs, and the resulting high-energy neutrinos stream out unimpeded. The authors compute the expected flux for the cosmologically preferred mass of 1.08 TeV, leaving the mass splitting free, and confront it with IceCube's non-observation of high-energy neutrinos from the Sun. The result is a robust bound of more than 566 keV on the splitting — comfortably above the roughly 350 keV that the LZ interpretation needed. It's a good example of how a signal-shaped hypothesis gets tested somewhere the original experiment never looked.

related.title: Could One Odd Recoil Be a Higgsino?
related.hook: LUX-ZEPLIN saw a single 248 keV nuclear recoil it couldn't explain away. Two theorists point out that a TeV-mass Higgsino would produce exactly that kind of event — with no free parameters to tune.

related.title: LZ's One Unexplained Recoil
related.hook: The world's most sensitive dark matter detector widened its search window and found exactly one hard nuclear recoil where almost no background should be. Not a discovery — but not nothing either.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the Sun a good dark matter detector even though we can't look inside it?
flashcards.back_html: Its gravity speeds dark matter up and its mass captures it. Trapped particles annihilate, and the resulting high-energy neutrinos pass straight out for detectors like IceCube to see.

flashcards.prompt: What does the Sun's gravity do that makes inelastic scattering possible in its core?

choices.text: Accelerates dark matter to about 1400 km/s, enough to pay the energy cost of the heavier state
Heats the dark matter until it decays
Compresses xenon nuclei so they scatter more strongly

flashcards.explanation_html: Inelastic scattering has an energy threshold set by the mass splitting. Solar infall boosts dark matter to roughly 1400 km/s, well above the local galactic speeds, so the reaction opens up.

flashcards.prompt: What limit does the IceCube non-observation place on the Higgsino mass splitting?
flashcards.back_html: Greater than 566 keV, for the cosmologically preferred mass of about 1.08 TeV — too large for the LZ event's inelastic interpretation to work.
